claim: Insects visually solve complex problems including the detection and tracking of fast moving prey.
source: Insects visually solve an array of complex problems including the detection and tracking of fast moving prey (Wiederman et al., 2017), long-distance navigation (Wehner, 2020), and even three-dimensional (3D) depth estimation (Nityananda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wiederman et al., 2017

claim: Insects perform long-distance navigation.
source: Insects visually solve an array of complex problems including the detection and tracking of fast moving prey (Wiederman et al., 2017), long-distance navigation (Wehner, 2020), and even three-dimensional (3D) depth estimation (Nityananda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wehner, 2020

claim: Insects perform three-dimensional depth estimation.
source: Insects visually solve an array of complex problems including the detection and tracking of fast moving prey (Wiederman et al., 2017), long-distance navigation (Wehner, 2020), and even three-dimensional (3D) depth estimation (Nityananda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nityananda et al., 2018

claim: The insect visual system is fundamentally different from that of mammals.
source: These capabilities are realised using a sensory apparatus that is fundamentally different from those of mammals.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about differences between insect and mammalian visual systems

claim: Each ommatidium features a lens, a light guide, and a cluster of photosensitive cells.
source: Each eye is constructed from a patchwork of self-contained light-sensing structures known as ommatidia, each featuring a lens, a light guide, and a cluster of photosensitive cells (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1a showing ommatidium structure

claim: Ommatidia are physically interlocked with their neighbours.
source: Ommatidia are physically interlocked with their neighbours, together forming a bulbous outer structure (the compound eye itself) that can vary in size, shape, and curvature, offering a range of adaptations for particular tasks and environments (Land and Nilsson, 2002; Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Land and Nilsson, 2002 and Figure 1b

claim: Compound eyes can vary in size, shape, and curvature, offering adaptations for particular tasks and environments.
source: Ommatidia are physically interlocked with their neighbours, together forming a bulbous outer structure (the compound eye itself) that can vary in size, shape, and curvature, offering a range of adaptations for particular tasks and environments (Land and Nilsson, 2002; Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Land and Nilsson, 2002

claim: The properties of the lens and photo-receptors are fixed for individual ommatidia but can vary across regions of an individual's eye.
source: The properties of the lens and photo-receptors are fixed for individual ommatidia but can vary across regions of an individual's eye (Meyer and Labhart, 1993) as well as between individuals of different castes (Collett and Land, 1975) and species (Land, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meyer and Labhart, 1993

claim: Ommatidial properties can vary between individuals of different castes.
source: The properties of the lens and photo-receptors are fixed for individual ommatidia but can vary across regions of an individual's eye (Meyer and Labhart, 1993) as well as between individuals of different castes (Collett and Land, 1975) and species (Land, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collett and Land, 1975

claim: Ommatidial properties can vary between species.
source: The properties of the lens and photo-receptors are fixed for individual ommatidia but can vary across regions of an individual's eye (Meyer and Labhart, 1993) as well as between individuals of different castes (Collett and Land, 1975) and species (Land, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Land, 1989

claim: The compound eye arrangement differs greatly from the mammalian system that utilises a single lens to project a high-resolution image onto a retina.
source: This arrangement of independent, interlocked light sensing elements and lenses differs greatly from the mammalian system that utilises a single lens to project a high-resolution image onto a retina.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of mammalian and insect visual system differences

claim: Wide field of view and low resolution benefit visual navigation.
source: Insights derived from this methodology include demonstration of the benefits of a wide field of view (FOV) and low resolution for visual navigation (Zeil et al., 2003; Vardy and Moller, 2005; Mangan and Webb, 2009; Wystrach et al., 2016), and the role played by non-visible light sensing for place recognition (Möller, 2002; Stone et al., 2006; Differt and Möller, 2016) and direction sensing (Lambrinos et al., 1997; Gkanias et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Zeil et al., 2003; Vardy and Moller, 2005; Mangan and Webb, 2009; Wystrach et al., 2016

claim: Non-visible light sensing plays a role in place recognition.
source: Insights derived from this methodology include demonstration of the benefits of a wide field of view (FOV) and low resolution for visual navigation (Zeil et al., 2003; Vardy and Moller, 2005; Mangan and Webb, 2009; Wystrach et al., 2016), and the role played by non-visible light sensing for place recognition (Möller, 2002; Stone et al., 2006; Differt and Möller, 2016) and direction sensing (Lambrinos et al., 1997; Gkanias et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Möller, 2002; Stone et al., 2006; Differt and Möller, 2016

claim: Non-visible light sensing plays a role in direction sensing.
source: Insights derived from this methodology include demonstration of the benefits of a wide field of view (FOV) and low resolution for visual navigation (Zeil et al., 2003; Vardy and Moller, 2005; Mangan and Webb, 2009; Wystrach et al., 2016), and the role played by non-visible light sensing for place recognition (Möller, 2002; Stone et al., 2006; Differt and Möller, 2016) and direction sensing (Lambrinos et al., 1997; Gkanias et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lambrinos et al., 1997; Gkanias et al., 2019

claim: All contemporary compound eye models sample from a single viewpoint.
source: Specifically, despite differences in the sampling techniques used (e.g. see Mangan and Webb, 2009; Baddeley et al., 2012 for custom sampling approaches, Neumann, 2002; Basten and Mallot, 2010 for rendering based cubemapping CEMs, and Polster et al., 2018 for ray-casting methods), all contemporary CEMs sample from a single viewpoint.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple CEM approaches and inference from the literature

claim: The distributed arrangement of ommatidia on distinct 3D eye surfaces provides insects with a multi-viewpoint system that generates different information for different eye shapes.
source: In contrast, the distributed arrangement of ommatidia on distinct 3D eye surfaces provides insects with a multi-viewpoint system that generates different information for different eye shapes.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the physical structure of compound eyes

claim: High-fidelity compound-vision rendering engines were developed previously but were not widely adopted.
source: High-fidelity compound-vision rendering engines with some of these features (though notably slower than real time) were developed previously (Giger, 1996; Collins, 1998; Polster et al., 2018) but were not widely adopted.
evidence: Supported by citations to Giger, 1996; Collins, 1998; Polster et al., 2018 and inference about adoption

claim: Previous high-fidelity compound-vision rendering engines were notably slower than real time.
source: High-fidelity compound-vision rendering engines with some of these features (though notably slower than real time) were developed previously (Giger, 1996; Collins, 1998; Polster et al., 2018) but were not widely adopted.
evidence: Supported by citations to Giger, 1996; Collins, 1998; Polster et al., 2018

claim: Dedicated ray-casting hardware allows for the capture of visual data from multiple locations in parallel at high speed.
source: Difficulties arising as a result of the computational complexity (and so execution time) of CEMs are diminishing as dedicated ray-casting hardware emerges that allows for the capture of visual data from multiple locations in parallel at high speed (e.g. Nvidia [Santa Clara, California, United States] RTX series GPUs [Purcell et al., 2005; Burgess, 2020]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Purcell et al., 2005; Burgess, 2020 and knowledge of GPU technology

claim: CompoundRay is capable of accurately rendering the visual perspective of bees with 6000 individual ommatidia arranged on 2 realistic eye surfaces at over 3000 frames per second.
source: This work introduces a new open-source CEM software (CompoundRay) that is capable of accurately rendering the visual perspective of bees (6000 individual ommatidia arranged on 2 realistic eye surfaces) at over 3000 frames per second.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Polygon projection-based rendering systems function by directly projecting the faces and vertices of the scene's 3D geometry through a singular imaging point and on to a projection plane.
source: As Figure 2a shows, these systems function by directly projecting the faces and vertices of the scene's 3D geometry through a singular imaging point and on to a projection plane.
evidence: Supported by Figure 2a and established knowledge of projection-based rendering

claim: Compound visual systems essentially form multiple pinhole-like viewing systems, each with their own image point.
source: In contrast, compound visual systems essentially form multiple pinhole-like viewing systems (Figure 2c), each with their own image point.
evidence: Supported by Figure 2c and inference from compound eye structure

claim: A polygon projection approach will struggle with optical phenomena involving multiple imaging points.
source: A polygon projection approach will struggle with these optical phenomena as the process directly transforms the faces of the 3D object from the scene onto the camera's view plane, in effect applying a projection transform onto a plane or other regular surface forming a singular image point (Figure 2a).
evidence: Based on inference from the limitations of projection-based rendering and reference to Figure 2a

claim: CompoundRay uses a ray-casting approach to rendering the insect visual perspective.
source: Drawing on previous work from Polster et al., 2018, CompoundRay uses a ray-casting approach to rendering the insect visual perspective.
evidence: Explicit statement about the software's methodology, with citation to Polster et al., 2018

claim: Ray-based methods allow for surfaces such as mirrors and lenses to accurately reflect light being rendered.
source: This allows for surfaces such as mirrors and lenses to accurately reflect light being rendered.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ray-based rendering capabilities

claim: Ray-based approaches can be incredibly computationally complex.
source: Ray-based approaches can be incredibly computationally complex, as each ray (of which there can be thousands per pixel) needs to be tested against every object in the scene (which can be composed of millions of objects) to detect and simulate interactions.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ray-based rendering computational requirements

claim: Ray-based rendering has historically only been used in offline cases where individual frames can take many hours to render.
source: Thus, they have historically only been used in offline cases where individual frames of an animation can take many hours to render, such as in cinema (Christensen et al., 2018), and prior to that in architectural and design drafting (Appel, 1968; Roth, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to Christensen et al., 2018; Appel, 1968; Roth, 1982

claim: GPU manufacturers have introduced dedicated programmable ray-tracing hardware into their graphics pipelines.
source: In order to better capture the photo-realistic offerings of ray-based rendering methods, GPU manufacturers have introduced dedicated programmable RT hardware into their graphics pipelines (Purcell et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Purcell et al., 2005 and knowledge of GPU technology

claim: RT cores are optimised for efficient parallel triangle-line intersection.
source: These RT cores are optimised for efficient parallel triangle-line intersection, allowing billions of rays to be cast in real time into complex 3D scenes.
evidence: Based on knowledge of RT core functionality

claim: It is practically infeasible to find a single projective transform to produce the appropriate composite view of compound eyes in a single projection-based operation.
source: These projection surfaces are often unique and varied, meaning it is practically infeasible to find a single projective transform to produce the appropriate composite view in a single projection-based operation.
evidence: Based on inference from the complexity of compound eye geometry

claim: Each individual ommatidium captures light from a cone of vision defined by the ommatidial acceptance angle.
source: Each individual ommatidium in a compound eye captures light from a cone of vision (defined by the ommatidial acceptance angle), much in the way that our own eyes observe only a forward cone of the world around us.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ommatidium function

claim: All light captured within the ommatidium's cone of vision is focused to a singular point on a small photo-receptor cluster.
source: However, in the case of the ommatidium, all light captured within the cone of vision is focused to a singular point on a small photo-receptor cluster, rather than the many millions of photo-receptors in the human eye that allow for the high-resolution image that we experience
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ommatidium structure and function

claim: CompoundRay uses Monte Carlo integration to estimate the light intensity from the scene within the ommatidium's sampling domain.
source: CompoundRay uses Monte Carlo integration (Kajiya, 1986) to estimate the light intensity from the scene within the ommatidium's sampling domain, effectively forming a small pinhole-type camera at the position of the ommatidium.
evidence: Explicit statement about the software's methodology with citation to Kajiya, 1986

claim: Previous works have implemented light sampling function approximation by assuming the influence of individual light rays is modulated dependent on the angle to the ommatidial axis via a Gaussian function.
source: Previous works Collins, 1998; Polster et al., 2018 have implemented this approximation of the light sampling function by assuming the influence of individual light rays, distributed statically across the sampling cone, is modulated dependent on the angle to the ommatidial axis via a Gaussian function with a full width at half maximum equal to the acceptance angle of the ommatidium, as seen in Figure 3a.
evidence: Supported by citations to Collins, 1998; Polster et al., 2018 and Figure 3a

claim: CompoundRay uses stochastic sampling direction modulation chosen at random in relation to the Gaussian probability curve on a frame-by-frame basis.
source: Instead, sampling direction is modulated and chosen at random in relation to the Gaussian probability curve of the sampling function on a temporal, frame-by-frame basis.
evidence: Explicit statement about the software's methodology

claim: Static sampling can result in elements of the scene being aliased out of the final measurement of sensed light.
source: Static sampling can result in elements of the scene (in the case demonstrated in Figure 3b, dark grey circles) being aliased out of the final measurement of sensed light.
evidence: Supported by demonstration in Figure 3b

claim: Stochastically varying the sampled direction on a frame-by-frame basis removes the structured nature of any single frame's aliasing.
source: Rather, by choosing to stochastically vary the sampled direction on a frame-by-frame basis removes the structured nature of any single frame's aliasing, as that same view point will generate different aliasing artefacts on the next frame, having the net effect of reducing structured aliasing when considering sequences of frames (Figure 3c).
evidence: Based on inference from stochastic sampling theory and supported by Figure 3c

claim: Averaging renderings from the same perspective becomes synonymous with an increased sampling rate.
source: One benefit of this approach is that averaging renderings from the same perspective becomes synonymous with an increased sampling rate, indeed, this is how the renderer increases sampling rate internally: by increasing the rendering volume for the compound perspective, effectively batch-rendering and averaging frames from the same point in time.
evidence: Based on inference from the stochastic sampling approach

claim: Each ommatidium will sample the simulated environment differently for every frame rendered, causing small variations in the colour received at any given ommatidium over time.
source: However, as each ommatidium will sample the simulated environment differently for every frame rendered, small variations in the colour received at any given ommatidium occur over time.
evidence: Based on inference from the stochastic sampling methodology

claim: The renderer is written in C++ and the Nvidia Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) GPU programming language.
source: The renderer is written in C++ and the Nvidia Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) GPU programming language and allows for a 3D environment representing a given experimental setup to be rendered from the perspective of an insect.
evidence: Explicit statement about the software implementation

claim: The core of the renderer runs in parallel on the GPU as a series of CUDA shader programs.
source: The core of the renderer runs in parallel on the GPU (the device) as a series of CUDA shader programs, which are driven by a C++ program running on the host computer (the host).
evidence: Explicit statement about the software architecture

claim: Environments are stored in GL Transmission Format (glTF) files.
source: Environments are stored in GL Transmission Format (glTF; Robinet et al., 2014) files consisting of 3D objects and cameras, the latter of which can be of two types: compound (structured sets of ommatidia) or traditional (perspective, orthographic, and panoramic).
evidence: Explicit statement about the software's file format with citation to Robinet et al., 2014

claim: The renderer is built on top of Nvidia's Optix ray-tracing framework.
source: The renderer is built on top of Nvidia's Optix (Parker et al., 2010) RT framework, which is a pipeline-based system: a pipeline is assembled, which then allows for parallel per-pixel rendering of the environment.
evidence: Explicit statement about the software foundation with citation to Parker et al., 2010

claim: Two pipelines are used in the renderer: an ommatidial pipeline and a display pipeline.
source: Two pipelines are used in the renderer: an ommatidial pipeline and a display pipeline.
evidence: Explicit statement about the software architecture

claim: The ommatidial pipeline handles sampling of the environment through the currently active compound eye.
source: The ommatidial pipeline handles sampling of the environment through the currently active compound eye, saving all samples from all ommatidia to a buffer stored within the eye's 'raw ommatidial view' portion of its data record.
evidence: Explicit statement about the software functionality

claim: The display pipeline handles the generation of the user-facing display buffer.
source: Conversely, the display pipeline handles the generation of the user-facing display buffer (Figure 4 –4).
evidence: Explicit statement about the software functionality with reference to Figure 4

claim: Using the glTF file format for scene storage allows the experimental configuration of 3D models, surface textures, and camera poses to be packed into a single file.
source: Using the glTF file format for scene storage allows the experimental configuration of 3D models, surface textures, and camera poses to be packed into a single file (although per-eye ommatidial configurations are stored separately as comma-separated value (CSV) files and linked to within the glTF file to avoid file bloat, retaining the readability of the glTF file).
evidence: Explicit statement about the software's file format capabilities

claim: The glTF format is a JSON-based human-readable file format for 3D scene storage that is readily supported by a number of popular 3D editors.
source: The glTF format is a JavaScript object notation (JSON)-based human-readable file format for 3D scene storage that is readily supported by a number of popular 3D editors and has allowances for extensions within its specification.
evidence: Based on knowledge of the glTF file format

claim: Three virtual eye models were created based on increasing simplifications of real-world eye data.
source: Three virtual eye models were created, based on increasing simplifications of real-world eye data.
evidence: Explicit statement about the experimental design

claim: The virtual eye models were assembled based on one Apis mellifera scan from eight scans of real-world samples taken by Baird and Taylor, 2017.
source: The virtual eye models were assembled based on one (Apis mellifera) of eight scans of real-world samples (two Apis mellifera, six Bombus terrestris) taken by Baird and Taylor, 2017, with the 3D surface shape used to derive sample points and axial directions for each of the 6374 ommatidia present in both eyes.
evidence: Explicit statement about the data source with citation to Baird and Taylor, 2017

claim: The real eye model contains 6374 ommatidia present in both eyes.
source: The virtual eye models were assembled based on one (Apis mellifera) of eight scans of real-world samples (two Apis mellifera, six Bombus terrestris) taken by Baird and Taylor, 2017, with the 3D surface shape used to derive sample points and axial directions for each of the 6374 ommatidia present in both eyes.
evidence: Explicit statement about the eye model specifications

claim: The 'split' and 'single' eye models were created to mimic assumptions made in past simulated compound vision studies.
source: These were created by editing the eye's ommatidial positions to either converge on two or one single point (Figure 5 i-iii, i-iii) to mimic assumptions made in past simulated compound vision studies (Franz et al., 1998; Baddeley et al., 2012; Nityananda et al., 2016; Polster et al., 2018).
evidence: Explicit statement with citations to Franz et al., 1998; Baddeley et al., 2012; Nityananda et al., 2016; Polster et al., 2018

claim: A multi-layer perceptron network with two fully connected hidden layers was trained to estimate the point's position as a proxy for the eye's ability to perform basic small-point spatial awareness tasks.
source: The three variations on the real eye design were then assessed against each other for their ability to resolve the 3D position of a target point within a simple black and white environment by training a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) network with two fully connected hidden layers to estimate the point's position, encoding the relationship between visual scene and relative location - a task that was taken as a proxy for the eye's ability to perform basic small-point spatial awareness tasks.
evidence: Explicit statement about the experimental methodology

claim: Comparing the views from varying ommatidial eye designs presents challenges due to differing surface shapes and ommatidial counts.
source: In particular, the differing surface shapes and ommatidial counts between any two eyes make direct comparison very challenging as a result of the lack of a one-to-one correspondence between the ommatidia of each eye.
evidence: Based on inference from the geometric differences between eye designs

claim: Small-point localisation was used as a basis for measuring eye utility because similar tasks have formed key parts of many behavioural studies.
source: In this example comparison method, we propose using the task of small-point localisation as a basis for measuring eye utility, as similar tasks have formed key parts of many behavioural studies (van Praagh et al., 1980; Juusola and French, 1997; Nityananda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Praagh et al., 1980; Juusola and French, 1997; Nityananda et al., 2016

claim: The non-Euclidian surface geometry of the compound eye makes convolutional neural network architectures inappropriate.
source: The non-Euclidian surface geometry of the compound eye makes convolutional neural network architectures (which typically operate over euclidian 2D or 3D space [Li et al., 2021]) inappropriate, as doing so would require a conversion from eye surface to a 2D surface, potentially introducing biases (as further elaborated in the 'Discussion' section).
evidence: Based on inference from the geometric properties of compound eyes and citation to Li et al., 2021

claim: Graph neural networks provide a method of operating over the 3D surface of the eye independent of assumptions of implicit spatially uniform sampling.
source: Graph neural networks (Scarselli et al., 2009) – neural networks that operate independent of assumptions of implicit spatially uniform sampling, instead operating over data structured in a graph – provide a method of operating over the 3D surface of the eye.
evidence: Supported by citation to Scarselli et al., 2009 and knowledge of graph neural networks

claim: The MLP network was designed with 2 hidden layers (1000 and 256 neurons) and a final linear output layer of 3 neurons.
source: We designed an MLP with 2 hidden layers (1000 and 256 neurons, with rectified linear activation functions to act as non-linearities) and a final linear output layer of 3 neurons to represent the x, y, and z components of the relative position vector.
evidence: Explicit statement about the neural network architecture

claim: For each eye design, 100,000 image position pairs were generated for training purposes.
source: For each eye design, 100,000 image position pairs were generated for training purposes. Of these, 80,000 were used for training, and 20,000 were used as a validation dataset in order to plot training progress.
evidence: Explicit statement about the experimental dataset

claim: Performance was benchmarked in two 3D environments: a lab environment and a 3D scan of a real-world natural environment.
source: Performance is benchmarked in two 3D environments: a lab environment inspired by those used in insect cognitive experiments (Ofstad et al., 2011); and a 3D scan of a real-world natural environment covering an area of a number of square kilometers.
evidence: Explicit statement about the benchmarking environments with citation to Ofstad et al., 2011

claim: The natural environment was constructed using structure-from-motion photogrammetry using photos captured from a drone over rural Harpenden, UK.
source: The natural environment was constructed using structure-from-motion photogrammetry using photos captured from a drone over rural Harpenden, UK (3D model subject to upcoming publication, available via contact of Dr. Joe Woodgate, Queen Mary University of London).
evidence: Explicit statement about the data collection methodology

claim: CompoundRay supports arbitrary arrangements of ommatidia within 3D space.
source: Criterion 1 states that the renderer must support arbitrary arrangements of ommatidia within 3D space. Figure 6 shows two different environments rendered using three differing eye designs, from a simple spherical model with spherical uniformly distributed ommatidia that more closely aligns with current compound eye rendering methods, to a hypothetical arbitrary arrangement similar to that of the now long-extinct Erbenochile erbeni.
evidence: Demonstrated by Figure 6 showing different eye designs

claim: It is possible to specify heterogeneous ommatidial optical properties across an eye in CompoundRay.
source: Criterion 2 states that it should be possible to specify heterogeneous ommatidial optical properties across an eye, such as the enlarged facets as found in robberflies (Wardill et al., 2017). As demonstrated in Figure 7, the renderer achieves this by allowing for shaping of the acceptance cone of each ommatidium.
evidence: Demonstrated by Figure 7 and citation to Wardill et al., 2017

claim: Heterogeneous ommatidial configurations are important for avoiding blind-spots and oversampling.
source: As can be seen in the generated image, this is important as it appropriately avoids creating blind-spots in the dorsal and ventral regions while also avoiding oversampling (blurring) in the horizontally acute region, resulting in a much clearer picture of the observed environment (before the visual data is passed into any insect visual processing neural circuits) while also minimising the required number of ommatidia.
evidence: Based on inference from the visual results shown in Figure 7

claim: The required number of samples per eye is highly positively correlated with the visual frequency and intensity of the simulated environment.
source: However, the required number of samples per eye is highly positively correlated with the visual frequency and intensity of the simulated environment at any given point, with locations exhibiting high contrast seen from a distance requiring higher sampling rates in order to properly resolve.
evidence: Based on inference from the sampling analysis

claim: A threshold of 1% was used, meaning that the maximum expected standard deviation of the most deviant ommatidium should be no greater than 1% of the maximum difference between two received colours.
source: Here, we use a threshold of 1%, meaning that the maximum expected standard deviation of the most deviant ommatidium on an eye (normalised to one steradian) should be no greater than 1% of the maximum difference between two received colours, here defined as the length of vector [255, 255, 255].
evidence: Explicit statement about the experimental threshold

claim: Performance improves significantly when the renderer is able to utilise the next-generation RT hardware available in the newer RTX series of NVidia graphics cards.
source: As can be seen, performance improves significantly when the renderer is able to utilise the next-generation RT hardware available in the newer RTX series of NVidia graphics cards, consistently outperforming older cards in the larger natural environment and outperforming in the smaller lab environment when using more than 30,000 rays.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10

claim: The previous generation of NVidia graphics cards was found to outperform the RTX series in the lab environment at lower ray counts (below 30,000).
source: Counterintuitively, the previous generation of NVidia graphics cards was found to outperform the RTX series in the (relatively small) lab environment at lower ray counts (below 30,000).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10

claim: Static overhead involved with the use of the RTX series' RT cores may cause the counterintuitive performance at lower ray counts.
source: This appears to be due to static overhead involved with the use of the RTX series' RT cores, which may also be the cause of the small positive trend seen between 1000 and 8000 samples when using the 2080Ti.
evidence: Based on speculation about the cause of observed performance patterns

claim: The 'real' eye design offers a higher utility (lower total error) when trying to locate the relative position of the sphere compared to both the 'split' and 'single' eye designs.
source: In terms of total error over the validation set, we observed that – as expected – the 'real' eye design appears to offer a higher utility (lower total error when trying to locate the relative position of the sphere), ultimately decreasing its network's validation error quicker and to a lower minimum after 100 epochs when compared to both the 'split' and 'single' eye designs (Figure 11a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11a

claim: The 'single' eye design eventually achieved a similar utility score on the validation set than that of the 'split' eye design.
source: Interestingly, despite an initial slow in learning rate, the 'single' eye design eventually achieved a similar utility score on the validation set than that of the 'split' eye design.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11a

claim: The most significant region of difference between the 'real' eye model and the 'single' eye model can be seen around the edges of the eye's field of vision.
source: Seemingly, the most significant region of difference between the 'real' eye model and the 'single' eye model can be seen around the edges of the eye's field of vision.
evidence: Based on analysis of the difference volumes shown in Figure 11b

claim: The difference between 'real' and 'single' eye models around the edges of the field of vision appears to be likely due to parallax.
source: As this difference follows the entirety of the edge of the eye's field of vision, this appears to be likely due to parallax – the 'real' eye samples from two points, allowing it slightly extended range of vision compared to that of the 'single' eye model, resulting in slightly different ranges of FOV between the two, with this difference increasing the further from the eye the point is.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed differences and knowledge of parallax effects

claim: There are two regions of higher error toward the forward-facing regions in the 'real' vs 'split' comparison.
source: In the 'real' vs 'split' comparison image, however, there are two regions of higher error (highlighted in red circles in Figure 11c) toward the forward-facing regions of the eye's vision.
evidence: Supported by visual data shown in Figure 11c

claim: The regions of higher error in the 'real' vs 'split' comparison indicate a region of improved visual information when using a full eye surface as compared to simple two-point sampling.
source: These indicate a region of improved visual information when using a full eye surface as compared to simple two-point sampling of the environment.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed differences in Figure 11c

claim: CompoundRay addresses the need for a fast, compound eye perspective rendering pipeline.
source: This paper has introduced a new compound eye perspective rendering software, CompoundRay, that addresses the need for a fast, compound eye perspective rendering pipeline (Stürzl et al., 2015; Taylor and Baird, 2017; Millward et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stürzl et al., 2015; Taylor and Baird, 2017; Millward et al., 2020

claim: CompoundRay can perform rendering tasks at speeds in the order of thousands of frames per second using consumer-grade graphics hardware.
source: In particular, the tool supports arbitrary instantiation of heterogeneous ommatidia at any place in space and can perform rendering tasks at speeds in the order of thousands of frames per second using consumer-grade graphics hardware.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: CompoundRay rendered over 3.3 million training images in only 2 hours.
source: For example, we used over 3.3 million training images, which CompoundRay rendered in only 2 hr.
evidence: Explicit statement about the software's performance

claim: CompoundRay can act as the previously missing step to integrate recently catalogued real eye designs into mapped insect environments.
source: In particular, CompoundRay can act as the previously missing step to integrate recently catalogued real eye designs (Baird and Taylor, 2017; Bagheri et al., 2020) into mapped insect environments (Stürzl et al., 2015; Risse et al., 2018) to explore the information provided to insects in their natural surroundings.
evidence: Supported by citations to Baird and Taylor, 2017; Bagheri et al., 2020; Stürzl et al., 2015; Risse et al., 2018

claim: The ability to configure ommatidial properties individually enables new investigations into the benefits of asymmetric compound eyes such as those found in robber flies and crabs.
source: Similarly, the ability to configure ommatidial properties individually and with respect to eye surface shape enables new investigations into the benefits of asymmetric compound eyes such as those found in robber flies (Wardill et al., 2017) and crabs (Zeil et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wardill et al., 2017 and Zeil et al., 1986

claim: CompoundRay can be used to model microsaccadic sampling in fruit flies.
source: Furthermore, we see opportunities to model the recently reported microsaccadic sampling in fruit flies (Juusola et al., 2017), as well as aid with similar vision-centric neurological studies (Viollet, 2014; Wystrach et al., 2016; Kemppainen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Juusola et al., 2017
